newsitem.title: USA: Mr Yen's point valid despite his retreat -analysts.
newsitem.headline: Mr Yen's point valid despite his retreat -analysts.

text.p: Despite repeated official denials that Japan has abandoned the G3 strong-dollar policy, the U.S. currency has yet to recover from its slide after Japanese finance minister Eisuke Sakakibara said its long climb against the yen was nearing an end.
Sakakibara was dubbed "Mr. Yen" for helping orchestrate the sharp dollar rally against the yen last year.
His recent remarks seemed intended to cap the dollar's rise for political reasons.
But they inadvertently alerted currency traders to a compelling economic argument against further dollar gains, economists said.

"I've always been skeptical of this Sakakibara yen rally -- doubtful that the politicians' voices over this matter in the long run," said Anil Kashyap, professor of economics in the Graduate School of Business at the University of Chicago.

Japan's economy is already set to emerge from six years of low growth without further yen depreciation that would put Japanese officials under even more pressure over Japan's persistent trade surplus with the United States.

"The yen is not likely to weaken further and if anything it will float around 110 (yen per dollar) for the foreseeable future," said Hugh Patrick, RD Calkins professor of international business at Columbia Business School.
"Lower (Japanese) interest rates are starting to work," he added.
Sandy Batten, international economist at Citibank, sees the dollar trading from 108 to 113 yen, with speculation over possible Japanese interest rate hikes providing volatility.

"We are going to see more of that (range) happening until the banking system and the economy gets in better shape to warrant an unwinding of this accommodative stance by the Bank of Japan," Batten said, adding he doesn't expect a monetary tightening until at least the middle of 1997.
Kashyap, while reluctant to make a short-term bet on the direction of dollar/yen, said: "The exchange rate has got to move back down to move towards correcting some of these trade flows."
Goldman, Sachs & Co research, as of November 12, forecast the dollar exchange rate will be at 112 yen in one month's time before steadily falling to 105 yen over the next 12 months.

Economists who foresee further dollar/yen gains said Japan is wearing a "monetary corset" as the official discount rate has stood at a historic low 0.50 percent for over a year. They also wonder whether Japan's government is prepared to adopt a fiscal policy that is free-spending enough to help.
"Yen devaluation remains the only economic policy option for the Hashimoto government," said Carl Weinberg, chief economist at High Frequency Economics Ltd.
"A yen devaluation affects an easing of overall monetary conditions, which is what is needed," he added.
Weinberg equated a 42 percent depreciation of the yen since May 1995 to a 1,400-basis-point cut in short-term interest rates.
But Columbia's Patrick sharply disagreed when asked if yen depreciation was the only tool left for Japan's economic engineers.
He said he viewed fiscal stimulus as more important than Japanese interest rates, adding that financial and business deregulation should also boost exports and the overall economy.

Chicago's Kashyap noted the relatively high level of reserves that banks have built up during a period of low interest rates. He said this gives officials the option of loosening bank credit flows to boost the economy.
"If you want to just look at the interest rate, I don't think that is a perfect indicator of the stance of monetary policy in Japan right now," he said.
"And for the idea that they are broke -- compare their fiscal situation to ours (the United States). They can certainly go ahead and pass a larger stimulus package if they choose to," he added.
The dollar, which hit a 42-month high of 114.92 yen on October 29, slid to its lowest level in almost a month at 111.27 yen on November 7 after the remarks from Sakakibara.
Dollar/yen's highest intraday level since then has been 111.96. The U.S. currency opened at 111.17 yen on Wednesday.

According to the Ministry of Finance, Japan's trade surplus with the U.S. expanded in October for the first time since February of 1995. The bilateral surplus grew 31.3 percent to 354.79 billion yen as Japanese car exports benefitted from a relatively weak yen.
The U.S. trade deficit with Japan shrunk a slight 0.3 percent in September to $3.79 billion from a revised $3.80 gap in August.
